stem: A finance team wants Claude to process vendor invoices. Every invoice goes through the same three steps: extract the line items, validate totals against the purchase order, then draft a ledger entry. The steps never change order, and the team wants predictable cost and easy auditing. Which design best fits?

options.text: An autonomous agent given all three tools and the goal, left to decide the order of steps for each invoice.
options.why: An agent adds variability, extra turns and cost to decide something that is already known; it trades away the predictability the team asked for.

options.text: A supervisor agent that dispatches each step to a separate specialist agent and merges their answers.
options.why: A multi-agent hierarchy is heavy machinery for a fixed three-step sequence and makes the flow harder, not easier, to audit.

options.text: A workflow that chains the three LLM calls in code, with programmatic checks between steps.
options.why: When the path is fixed and known in advance, a predefined workflow (prompt chaining with gates) gives predictable cost, latency and an auditable sequence.

options.text: One large prompt that asks Claude to do all three steps and return the ledger entry at the end.
options.why: Collapsing the steps removes the intermediate checkpoints where validation can catch an extraction error before it reaches the ledger.

explanation: Workflows orchestrate LLM calls through predefined code paths and suit tasks whose steps are known in advance; agents let the model direct its own process and suit open-ended tasks. A fixed extract-validate-draft pipeline is a textbook prompt chain with programmatic gates between steps.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents

stem: A platform team wants Claude to investigate incoming bug reports across dozens of services. Some reports are resolved by reading one log file; others require searching code, reproducing the issue, and checking recent deploys. The number and order of steps cannot be predicted in advance. Which approach best fits?

options.text: An agent that picks its own tool calls in a loop, bounded by a turn limit and a human review point.
options.why: Open-ended problems with an unpredictable number of steps are where agents fit; guardrails such as turn limits and checkpoints keep the autonomy bounded.

options.text: A routing workflow that classifies each report into one of five fixed categories with a hard-coded handler each.
options.why: Routing helps when inputs fall into known categories with known handling; here the investigation path itself varies per report.

options.text: A prompt chain with four fixed steps: read logs, search code, check deploys, write summary.
options.why: Forcing every report through the same four steps wastes work on easy reports and still cannot adapt when a report needs a step not in the chain.

options.text: A single call that includes all logs, code and deploy history in context and asks for a diagnosis.
options.why: Pre-loading everything is infeasible across dozens of services and leaves the model unable to gather the specific evidence each report needs.

explanation: Agents are the right choice when the problem is open-ended and the steps cannot be hard-coded, provided the environment gives feedback (tool results) and the autonomy is bounded by stopping conditions and checkpoints. Fixed chains and routers work only when the path or the categories are known in advance.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents

stem: A team built a customer-operations system from four peer agents (billing, shipping, returns, account) that can message each other freely. In production, conversations bounce between agents, some loops never end, and no one can tell which agent owns the final answer. What should the team change first?

options.text: Give every agent access to all four tool sets so any agent can finish a request without handing it off.
options.why: Merging all tools into every agent removes specialization and widens each agent's permissions without fixing who owns the outcome.

options.text: Add a sentence to every agent's prompt asking it to avoid passing requests back and forth.
options.why: A prompt request does not create a control structure; nothing enforces ownership or terminates the loops.

options.text: Switch all four agents to the largest model tier so they coordinate more intelligently.
options.why: A stronger model does not fix an architecture in which no component is responsible for planning, delegation and termination.

options.text: Add a supervisor agent that plans each request, delegates to specialists, and owns the final answer.
options.why: A supervisor/orchestrator hierarchy gives a single owner for planning and the final response, and workers report back to it instead of to each other.

explanation: In a manager/supervisor hierarchy, one orchestrator decomposes the task, delegates scoped work to specialist workers, collects their results and decides when the task is done. That structure removes ownerless peer-to-peer loops and makes traces easy to follow.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (orchestrator-workers)

stem: An architect is deciding whether a research assistant should use a lead agent that spawns subagents instead of a single agent. In which two situations do subagents most clearly improve task execution? (Choose two.)

options.text: Several workers must make small, interdependent edits to the same file in a strict sequence.
options.why: Tightly coupled, sequential edits to shared state need close coordination; splitting them across subagents invites conflicts and lost context.

options.text: The question breaks into independent research threads that can be explored in parallel.
options.why: Independent, breadth-first subtasks parallelize well, so subagents can cut wall-clock time and explore more ground.

options.text: Each thread produces large volumes of raw search output, but the lead agent needs only condensed findings.
options.why: Subagents work in their own context windows and return summaries, keeping verbose intermediate output out of the lead agent's context.

options.text: The main goal is to minimize total token spend compared with a single agent.
options.why: Multi-agent systems usually consume more total tokens than a single agent; the gains are in speed, breadth and context isolation, not cost.

options.text: The lead agent wants to skip writing task briefs because subagents already see its full history.
options.why: Subagents start from their own context; the delegating agent must pass a clear objective, scope and output format.

explanation: Subagents pay off when work can be split into independent pieces (parallelism) and when isolating each piece in its own context window keeps the orchestrator focused on distilled results. They add token cost and coordination overhead, so they fit poorly for tightly coupled work or cost-minimization goals.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: In an orchestrator-worker system, the orchestrator delegates "look into competitor pricing" to three worker subagents. Two workers return overlapping results and the third researches a different product line entirely. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Let the workers share one conversation history so they can see and avoid each other's work.
options.why: Sharing one history removes the context isolation that makes workers useful and still leaves the task itself underspecified.

options.text: Have the orchestrator give each worker a distinct objective, clear scope limits, and an output format.
options.why: Vague delegation causes duplicated and off-target work; explicit objectives, boundaries and output formats let each worker do a distinct, useful slice.

options.text: Increase the number of workers so that the correct product line is more likely to be covered by at least one.
options.why: Adding more workers with the same vague brief multiplies duplication and cost instead of fixing the delegation.

options.text: Replace the workers with a single agent that has a larger max_tokens value.
options.why: max_tokens caps output length; it does not address how the task was divided or described.

explanation: Subagents only know what the orchestrator tells them. Clear delegation, with a specific objective, what is in and out of scope, which tools or sources to use, and what shape to return, is what prevents duplicated effort and drift.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: A support chatbot must answer within a few seconds. About 90% of messages are order-status, password-reset, or refund-policy questions with well-understood handling; the remaining 10% are unusual multi-step problems. Leadership wants low latency and cost without failing the hard cases. Which architecture best balances these constraints?

options.text: Send every message to a tool-using agent so that easy and hard cases are all handled uniformly by one path.
options.why: Running an open-ended agent loop on routine questions adds latency and cost for no benefit on 90% of traffic.

options.text: Handle the three common intents with fixed flows and reply to everything else with a canned apology.
options.why: This meets the latency goal but abandons the hard cases, which the requirement says must not fail.

options.text: Route each message: known intents go to fixed workflows, and unrecognized ones escalate to an agent.
options.why: A routing step sends predictable traffic down cheap, fast paths and reserves agent autonomy for the cases that actually need it.

options.text: Use a supervisor with specialist subagents for every message so each intent gets an expert.
options.why: A multi-agent hierarchy on every message maximizes latency and cost, the opposite of what the routine 90% needs.

explanation: Architecture choices can be mixed: a router workflow classifies inputs and dispatches known categories to deterministic handlers while escalating open-ended cases to an agent. This keeps the common path fast and cheap and applies autonomy only where the task is unpredictable.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (routing)

stem: A developer wants to embed a coding agent inside an existing Python service. The agent must read and edit files, run shell commands, respect permission rules, and support hooks, and the developer does not want to write the tool-execution loop or context management from scratch. Which option best fits?

options.text: The Claude client SDK calling the Messages API, with custom code for each tool and for the agent loop itself.
options.why: This works but means building the agent loop, file and shell tools, permissions and context handling yourself, which the developer wants to avoid.

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which exposes Claude Code's agent loop, built-in tools and hooks as a library.
options.why: The Agent SDK provides the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, programmable from Python or TypeScript in your own process.

options.text: The Message Batches API, submitting each file operation as a separate batched request.
options.why: Batches are for asynchronous, independent requests; they provide no tool execution or interactive agent loop.

options.text: An interactive Claude Code terminal session that developers run by hand when the service needs it.
options.why: An interactive terminal session is not embedded in the service and cannot be called programmatically as part of its request flow.

explanation: The Claude Agent SDK is a library that runs Claude Code's agent harness, including built-in tools, permissions, sessions and hooks, inside an application you operate. The client SDK gives raw API access where you write the loop yourself, and Batches is an asynchronous bulk-processing API.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs — Overview

stem: A developer is writing a custom agent loop directly on the Messages API with client-side tools. Which loop structure is correct?

options.text: Stop looping as soon as a response contains any text block, since a text block means Claude has finished answering.
options.why: A response can contain explanatory text alongside tool_use blocks; stopping on text would drop pending tool calls.

options.text: Put each tool's output in the system prompt of the next request so Claude can reference it.
options.why: Tool output belongs in tool_result content blocks in the conversation, tied to the call that requested it, not in the system prompt.

options.text: Start a fresh single-message request for each tool call that contains only that tool's output.
options.why: Dropping the prior turns loses the task, the tool_use block and all earlier reasoning, so Claude cannot continue coherently.

options.text: While stop_reason is "tool_use", run the tools, send tool_result blocks in a user turn, and repeat (with a turn cap).
options.why: This is the standard loop: execute requested tools, return results matched by tool_use_id, and repeat until Claude ends its turn, with a cap as a safety stop.

explanation: A custom harness drives the loop by checking stop_reason. When it is "tool_use", the application executes each requested tool, appends the assistant turn plus a user turn with tool_result blocks referencing each tool_use_id, and calls the API again. A maximum-iteration limit keeps runaway loops bounded.
reference: Claude API docs — Tool use: handle tool calls

stem: A startup wants agents that run for minutes to hours, executing code and browsing the web in a secure sandbox, with session history persisted server-side. The team is small and does not want to build or operate an agent loop, sandbox, or tool-execution layer. Which deployment model best fits?

options.text: Claude Managed Agents, using Anthropic-hosted sessions that run in a managed cloud sandbox.
options.why: Managed Agents provides a hosted harness, sandboxed tool execution and persisted session events, which suits long-running, asynchronous work with minimal infrastructure.

options.text: A custom agent loop on the Messages API, deployed and operated on the team's own container cluster.
options.why: A self-built loop gives maximum control but requires exactly the harness, sandbox and state management the team wants to avoid.

options.text: The Agent SDK running on a developer laptop, restarted manually when a task is needed.
options.why: A laptop process is neither managed infrastructure nor a reliable host for hours-long unattended sessions.

options.text: The Message Batches API with web search enabled, polling results the next day.
options.why: Batches runs independent requests asynchronously; it does not provide a persistent sandbox or an interactive, steerable agent session.

explanation: Anthropic-hosted Managed Agents supplies the agent harness and infrastructure (sandbox, built-in tools, persisted sessions and event streams), so teams do not build their own loop. Self-hosting a custom loop or the Agent SDK trades that convenience for control over runtime and infrastructure.
reference: Claude Managed Agents docs — Overview

stem: A bank wants to adopt Claude Managed Agents for its hosted harness and session management, but compliance requires that all code execution and file access happen on infrastructure the bank controls. Which configuration meets both goals with the least custom engineering?

options.text: Use Managed Agents with the default Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox and restrict all tools to read-only access.
options.why: Read-only tools still execute in Anthropic's sandbox, so file access does not happen on bank-controlled infrastructure.

options.text: Use Managed Agents with an environment configured as a self-hosted sandbox on the bank's infrastructure.
options.why: Managed Agents environments can point to a self-hosted sandbox, keeping tool execution in-house while Anthropic still runs the harness and sessions.

options.text: Rebuild the full agent loop, tool layer and session store on the Messages API inside the bank's VPC.
options.why: This satisfies the execution constraint but throws away the hosted harness the bank wanted, maximizing custom engineering.

options.text: Have employees run Claude Code interactively on their workstations instead of deploying agents.
options.why: Interactive workstation sessions do not provide a deployable, centrally managed agent service.

explanation: Deployment models form a spectrum: fully Anthropic-hosted (harness plus cloud sandbox), hosted harness with a self-hosted sandbox, or fully self-hosted (Agent SDK or a custom loop). When only execution must stay in-house, a self-hosted sandbox behind the hosted harness meets compliance without rebuilding the harness.
reference: Claude Managed Agents docs — Self-hosted sandboxes

stem: A team's Agent SDK coding agent is told in its system prompt to "never modify .env files" and to "always run the formatter after editing." Logs show both instructions are occasionally ignored. The team needs these rules to hold every time. What should they do?

options.text: Move both rules to the top of the system prompt and write them in capital letters.
options.why: Stronger wording may improve compliance but is still a probabilistic request, not a guarantee.

options.text: Add a final step asking the agent to review its own changes for .env edits and missed formatting.
options.why: Self-review is another model judgment that can miss violations; it does not deterministically block or run anything.

options.text: Add a PreToolUse hook that denies .env edits and a PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter.
options.why: Hooks run in the harness on every matching event, so the block and the formatter run deterministically regardless of what the model decides.

options.text: Lower the temperature so the agent follows its system prompt more consistently.
options.why: Lower temperature reduces sampling variety but does not turn instructions into enforced rules.

explanation: Hooks are callbacks the harness runs at defined lifecycle points. A PreToolUse hook can inspect a tool call and deny it, and a PostToolUse hook can run follow-up actions such as formatting or audit logging. Use hooks for rules that must always hold; use prompts for guidance.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs — Hooks

stem: An Agent SDK coding agent must meet several requirements every time, not just when the model remembers. The developer is mapping each requirement to a hook event. Which two mappings are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A PostToolUse hook that replaces tool output with a copy that has API keys redacted, before Claude reads it.
options.why: PostToolUse runs after the tool executes and can replace the output Claude sees, so secrets are removed deterministically before they reach the context.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that redacts API keys from each tool's output before Claude reads that output.
options.why: PreToolUse runs before the tool executes, so there is no output yet to redact; it is the event for inspecting, modifying or blocking the call itself.

options.text: A PreCompact hook that archives the full transcript before older history is summarized away.
options.why: PreCompact fires before compaction replaces history with a summary, which is exactly when a complete copy of the transcript must be saved.

options.text: A Stop hook that blocks destructive shell commands before the agent is able to run them.
options.why: Stop fires when the agent finishes its run; blocking a command has to happen in PreToolUse, before the tool executes.

options.text: A UserPromptSubmit hook that runs the code formatter after every file the agent edits.
options.why: UserPromptSubmit fires when a prompt is submitted, not after edits; a formatter belongs in a PostToolUse hook matched to the edit tools.

explanation: Hooks make actions deterministic, but only if they are attached to the right lifecycle event. PreToolUse can inspect, modify or deny a call before it runs; PostToolUse can act on or replace a tool's result; PreCompact runs before history is summarized; Stop runs when the agent finishes. Picking the event whose timing matches the requirement is part of designing a harness.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs — Hooks (available hooks)

stem: A custom agent harness occasionally runs for hundreds of turns on one task, calling the same search tool with near-identical queries and running up large bills. The team needs to contain the damage quickly while they investigate the root cause. What should they add to the harness first?

options.text: A per-task turn and spend budget, plus detection of repeated identical tool calls that stops the run.
options.why: A harness-level budget and repetition check deterministically caps runaway loops no matter why the model is repeating itself.

options.text: A higher max_tokens value so that each response has more room to reason its way out of the loop.
options.why: max_tokens limits the length of one response; it does not bound the number of loop iterations or their cost.

options.text: A temperature of 0 so the model stops producing slightly different queries each turn.
options.why: Deterministic sampling can make the repetition more exact rather than stopping it, and it sets no upper bound on turns.

options.text: A move to the largest model tier on the assumption that a stronger model will not get stuck this way.
options.why: A larger model may loop less often but provides no guaranteed limit and increases the cost of each iteration.

explanation: The harness owns the loop, so it is the right place for stopping conditions: maximum turns, spend or time budgets, and detection of repeated actions. These guardrails bound cost immediately; diagnosing why the model repeats (for example, unhelpful tool results) comes next.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs — Agent loop

stem: In a tool-use loop, Claude returns one assistant message containing three tool_use blocks: two weather lookups and one calendar lookup. How should the application return the results?

options.text: Send three separate user messages, one per tool_result, in the order the tools finished.
options.why: Splitting results across several user turns breaks the expected structure; the results for one assistant turn belong together.

options.text: Return only the first tool's result, then wait for Claude to request the others again.
options.why: Every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result; omitting results leaves the calls unanswered.

options.text: Concatenate all three outputs into one plain-text user message without tool_use_id references.
options.why: Plain text loses the tool_use_id link, so Claude cannot reliably tell which output belongs to which call.

options.text: Send one user message containing three tool_result blocks, each referencing its tool_use_id.
options.why: Parallel tool calls are answered in a single user turn with one tool_result per call, each tied to its request by tool_use_id.

explanation: Claude can request several tools in one turn. The application runs them (in parallel if it wishes) and returns all results in the next user message as tool_result blocks, each carrying the matching tool_use_id, before calling the API again.
reference: Claude API docs — Tool use: parallel tool use

stem: A long-running research agent makes dozens of tool calls per task. Late in each task, the context is dominated by old search results the agent no longer needs, and answer quality drops before the context limit is even reached. Which context-management approach is most effective?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window and keep the full history.
options.why: A bigger window delays the limit but leaves the context cluttered with stale results that dilute attention.

options.text: Clear stale tool results and compact older turns into a summary, keeping the task and recent turns.
options.why: Removing stale tool output and summarizing history keeps the context focused on what still matters without losing the goal.

options.text: Drop the oldest messages first whenever the conversation grows past a fixed token count, keeping only the newest.
options.why: Blind truncation from the front tends to discard the original task and key decisions first.

options.text: Restart the agent every ten turns with an empty history and the original prompt.
options.why: Restarting without carried-over state throws away progress and forces the agent to redo work.

explanation: Context is a finite attention budget, and quality can degrade as it fills with irrelevant tokens. Effective patterns include clearing tool results that have served their purpose and compacting older history into summaries, while preserving the task definition, key decisions and recent turns.
reference: Anthropic — Effective context engineering for AI agents

stem: A personal assistant agent should remember each user's preferences and past project decisions across sessions that may be days apart. Which pattern best provides this memory?

options.text: A persistent memory store the agent reads and writes via a tool, loading relevant entries at session start.
options.why: External memory survives between sessions and lets the agent retrieve only relevant facts rather than the whole history.

options.text: Rely on the model to recall the user from earlier sessions, because it has already seen their messages before.
options.why: The model is stateless between requests; it retains nothing from prior sessions unless the application supplies it.

options.text: Replay every past transcript in full at the start of each new session.
options.why: Replaying everything grows without bound, wastes tokens and buries the few facts that matter.

options.text: Fine-tune a model each week on the week's conversations for every user.
options.why: Per-user fine-tuning is slow, costly and unsuited to facts that change daily; memory belongs in retrievable storage.

explanation: Because the model keeps no state between calls, cross-session memory is an application pattern: store durable facts outside the context window (files, a database, or a memory tool) and retrieve what is relevant at the right time. This keeps context small and memory current.
reference: Claude API docs — Memory tool

stem: A team is comparing agent frameworks to use with Claude for multi-step tasks. Which three statements accurately describe these frameworks at a conceptual level? (Choose three.)

options.text: LangGraph models an app as a graph of nodes and edges over shared state, suiting explicit branches and loops.
options.why: LangGraph's core abstraction is a stateful graph, giving developers explicit control over control flow, cycles and checkpoints.

options.text: Using any of these frameworks removes the need to handle tool errors or to build evaluations yourself.
options.why: Frameworks provide structure, not correctness; tool failures and evaluation remain the developer's responsibility.

options.text: PydanticAI centers on typed Python models to define and validate structured agent inputs and outputs.
options.why: PydanticAI builds on Pydantic, so type-checked, validated structured outputs are a central feature.

options.text: These frameworks work only with their own vendor's models, so using Claude requires a separate, dedicated stack.
options.why: All three are model-agnostic and support Claude through provider integrations.

options.text: Strands Agents is model-driven: you supply a model, a prompt and tools, and the model drives the loop.
options.why: Strands emphasizes letting the model plan and call tools in a loop rather than having the developer hard-code the flow.

options.text: A framework guarantees deterministic results for the same input, which direct API calls cannot provide.
options.why: Frameworks orchestrate calls to the same non-deterministic models; they do not make outputs deterministic.

explanation: Agent frameworks package common patterns: LangGraph emphasizes explicit, stateful graph control flow; PydanticAI emphasizes typed, validated structured data; Strands emphasizes a model-driven tool loop. None removes the need for error handling or evaluation, and none makes model output deterministic.
reference: Framework documentation — LangGraph, PydanticAI, Strands Agents

stem: A developer needs Claude to extract fields from support emails using one lookup tool, a job that takes one or two tool calls. A teammate proposes adopting a full agent-graph framework "so we are ready to scale." The team has little time for debugging and wants to see exactly what is sent to the model. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Adopt the framework now, because migrating an existing codebase to it later would be harder than starting with it.
options.why: Premature abstraction adds layers that hide prompts and responses, making a simple task harder to debug for speculative future benefit.

options.text: Build a supervisor with extraction and lookup subagents to prepare for future growth.
options.why: A multi-agent design adds latency, cost and failure points to a task a single call handles.

options.text: Avoid tools entirely and paste the lookup data into every prompt instead.
options.why: This trades a clean tool call for stale, bloated context and does not address the framework question.

options.text: Call the API directly with a simple tool loop, and adopt a framework only when complexity demands it.
options.why: Starting simple keeps prompts and responses visible and easy to debug; a framework can be added once the workflow truly needs it.

explanation: Frameworks can speed up complex agent work, but they add abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts and responses and tempt teams into unnecessary complexity. For a small, well-defined task, direct API use with a simple loop is easier to understand and debug.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (when and how to use frameworks)

stem: A coding agent must find the root cause of a production error by scanning roughly 200 large log files, then fix the code. When it reads the logs itself, its context fills with log text and it loses track of the codebase details it needs for the fix. What should the developer do?

options.text: Tell the agent to read the logs more quickly and skip lines it considers unimportant.
options.why: Skimming still pulls large volumes of log text into the same context and relies on the model to discard it.

options.text: Load all 200 logs into the first prompt so the agent sees everything before it starts working on the fix.
options.why: Front-loading the logs makes the context problem worse and may exceed the context window outright.

options.text: Delegate the log search to a subagent that uses its own context and returns a concise summary.
options.why: A subagent keeps the verbose log output in its own context window and hands the main agent just the findings it needs.

options.text: Increase max_tokens so the agent has more room for the logs and the fix.
options.why: max_tokens limits output length; it does not enlarge the context window or reduce what the logs consume.

explanation: The subagent pattern isolates noisy, high-volume work, such as log scans, broad searches or test runs, in a separate context and returns a distilled result. The main agent keeps its context for the reasoning and editing that follow.
reference: Claude Code docs — Subagents

stem: An agent is migrating 300 source files to a new API. The work spans many context windows, and after each compaction or restart the agent sometimes redoes finished files or skips others. Which two practices most improve continuity across context windows? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep a progress file of completed, in-progress and remaining files, and read it at every start.
options.why: Structured state kept outside the context window lets a fresh window pick up exactly where the last one stopped.

options.text: Disable compaction so the agent keeps the entire migration history in one window from start to finish.
options.why: A 300-file migration will not fit in one window; turning off compaction just causes a hard failure when the window fills.

options.text: Commit and run tests after each batch so each new window can check real state in git and test results.
options.why: Commits and tests are durable checkpoints that show what is actually done, independent of what the model remembers.

options.text: Rely on the model to recall which files it already finished during earlier context windows.
options.why: Once earlier turns are compacted or dropped, the model cannot recall details that are no longer in context.

options.text: Paste all 300 files into the first prompt so that later windows already know the full scope.
options.why: That floods the first window and does nothing to carry progress forward into later windows.

explanation: Long-horizon agents need memory outside the context window. Progress notes or task lists, together with verifiable checkpoints such as commits and test results, let each new window reconstruct state reliably instead of depending on recall.
reference: Anthropic — Effective harnesses for long-running agents
